subject: chemistry-1
question: A physiology text lists the normal serum reference interval for the major extracellular cation as 135-145 mEq/L. Which ion is being described, and what is the midpoint of that interval?

options.text: Potassium (K+), midpoint 140 mEq/L, because K+ is the dominant cation of extracellular fluid
Calcium (Ca2+), midpoint 140 mEq/L, because Ca2+ is the chief cation dissolved in plasma
Sodium (Na+), midpoint 140 mEq/L, because Na+ is the dominant cation of extracellular fluid
Sodium (Na+), midpoint 280 mEq/L, because the two interval endpoints are added together

explanation:
Sodium is the principal extracellular cation, and the midpoint of its reference interval is the mean of the endpoints: (135 + 145)/2 = 140 mEq/L. Adding the endpoints without dividing gives 280, a unit-nonsensical value. Potassium is the principal intracellular cation and circulates at only about 3.5-5 mEq/L, and although calcium is the most abundant cation in the body by mass, over 99% of it is bound in bone rather than dissolved in plasma (total serum calcium is roughly 4.5-5.5 mEq/L).

ELI-10: Two separate skills are being checked. The identity part rests on compartments: sodium is concentrated in the fluid outside cells, potassium inside cells, which is why a blood sample is dominated by sodium. The arithmetic part is a midpoint, which is an average, not a sum: add 135 and 145 to get 280, then divide by 2 to get 140. Forgetting the division is the classic slip, and 280 mEq/L should look wrong immediately because it sits far outside any plausible serum value.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
